validator: draft 1 passed with no problems, soft problems or warnings
keep: The idea is named in the first three sentences: a gear pair or belt trades speed for torque by one ratio, and the power passes through less a small loss.

The speed rule is derived, not asserted: same-size teeth, one tooth past the mesh on each gear, so the 20-tooth pinion turns five times per turn of the 100-tooth wheel and both gears' teeth move at 6.1 m/s at the mesh.

The torque rule is derived from the push at the mesh: 72.4 N m ÷ 0.04 m = 1811 N, the same push on the wheel's tooth 0.2 m out, 362 N m. Moments and Newton's third law carry it, with nothing taken on trust. P = Tω then shows the power unchanged.
It answers the course's puzzle directly: the slow shaft and its coupling carry almost five times the torque, so they are the thick ones.

Every brief misconception has a DO screen with its own wrong pick: power multiplied by the ratio (6), torque passed through unchanged (4, 12), ratio upside down (2, 10), compound ratios added (8), rev/min left in (12), parallel shafts taken as aligned (13).
Thirteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and end on two mixed puzzles (12, 13).

The analogy is from his trade, a step-down transformer, and keeps the main result: voltage ÷ ratio, current × ratio, power through less a loss, thicker conductor on the high-current side. Its break is correct science.
fix: False absolute: 'A gear pair turns its gears opposite ways' is untrue of a ring gear meshing on its inside. Say two gears meshing on their outsides turn opposite ways.
False absolute: 'A belt turns both pulleys the same way' is untrue of a crossed belt. Say an open belt does.
Causal step skipped: 'teeth the same size, so tooth count grows with size' skips that the teeth sit evenly round the rim, so the count goes with the distance round it, which goes with the diameter.

Causal step blurred: 'the wheel's tooth is pushed with the same 1811 N' cites Newton's third law for the wrong pair. Say the pinion's tooth pushes the wheel's tooth with that 1811 N, and the wheel's tooth pushes back just as hard, which is the load the motor feels.

Brief shows the effect without its cause: it names the speed falling and torque rising but not the shared speed at the mesh. Add that the teeth keep one speed at the mesh, and phrase the action as adding teeth to the wheel.

Check tests recall: screen 6 asks 11 kW through a 5 : 1 box at 95%, the very case screen 5 has just shown. Use a new case: 15 kW into a 4 : 1 box at 96% gives 14.4 kW, with wrong picks 60 kW (power × ratio) and 15 kW (loss left out).

Talks about the idea: 'Here is why it works, and why the slow shaft must be the strong one' signposts instead of teaching, and 'You have met a 5 : 1 reduction' points back at an earlier lesson. State the reduction itself and go straight to the reason.
Claim wider than true: 'That is why the slow shaft is the thicker one' becomes 'usually the thicker one', as the course's puzzle says.

shape.rule stated in words: yes: the speed divides by the ratio, the torque multiplies by it, the power out is the power in × the efficiency
shape.one worked example with real numbers: yes: the 11 kW, 1450 rev/min motor through 20 and 100 teeth, and a 7.5 kW hoist drive in practice
shape.misconception shown failing: yes: the power bar never grows (screens 5 and 6), torque passed through unchanged (4, 12), compound ratios added (8)
shape.analogy with where it breaks: yes: a step-down transformer, which needs alternating current and has no sliding teeth
shape.put it into practice: yes: safe way first, steps, rules of thumb, worked example, mistakes
